activities.anchor: Three things, always the same three
activities.caption: pair each input with the job it does in the bean's cup
activities.name: agThreeInputsMatch

config.prompt: Three inputs, three jobs. Match the input to the work it does:

pairs.right: the delivery service — carries dissolved goods up from the roots
the warehouse and anchor — holds the plant upright and stores nutrients

config.why: Nothing was added to the cup — the bean spent only what the cup already held: light for power, water for delivery, soil for support and minerals.

activities.anchor: This shape is called a Mitscherlich-style
activities.caption: which curve is the Mitscherlich response?
activities.name: agResponseTrace

config.prompt: Four candidate shapes for 'yield against nitrogen applied'. Which one is the Mitscherlich-style response the lesson describes?

curves.label: steep, then bending and flattening toward a ceiling
flat, then curving upward faster and faster

config.why: Yield rises steeply, bends, then flattens toward the r_max ceiling. That bend — not the ceiling — is where diminishing returns begin, and every later section of the lesson is another way of reading it.

activities.anchor: match the land to its capability, rotate crops
activities.caption: file each management move — building soil capital or spending it?
activities.name: agCapitalBuckets

config.prompt: The lesson calls the soil a living asset with organic matter as its capital. File each practice:
config.why: Cover crops and returned residues feed the biology and build crumb structure; compaction, bare fallow and over-tillage oxidise organic matter and collapse the water-holding benefit it bought.

activities.anchor: roughly 160 kg of nitrogen
activities.caption: find the faulty line in this nutrient-balance working
activities.name: agWithdrawalSpot

config.prompt: A student balances a field's nutrient account. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: Rule: the harvest is a withdrawal — every tonne of grain exports nutrients off the field.
A wheat crop yielding 8 t/ha removes about 160 kg of nitrogen in the grain alone.
Nothing else leaves the field, so nitrogen is the only nutrient to replace.
Therefore sustainable farming is an accountant's discipline: replace what you export.
If exports are not replaced, the soil's balance sheet goes negative within a decade.
config.correction: Wheat removes appreciable phosphorus and potassium as well as nitrogen — several nutrient accounts need replacing, not just one.
config.why: The lesson's figure is 'roughly 160 kg of nitrogen, plus appreciable phosphorus and potassium, in the grain alone'. Treating nitrogen as the only withdrawal under-counts the export.

activities.anchor: Waterlogged roots cannot breathe
activities.caption: true or false — the price of over-watering
activities.name: agWaterJudge

statements.s: A plant can only take up nutrients that are dissolved in soil water.
statements.why: Nutrients move through soil solution, not dry soil — water is the delivery service.

statements.s: More irrigation always means a bigger harvest.
statements.why: Waterlogged roots cannot breathe, and salts left behind as water evaporates slowly salinise the soil — over-irrigation backfires.

statements.s: Roughly 1,000–2,000 litres of water go into a kilo of wheat grain.
statements.why: That is the lesson's figure, counting everything the crop transpired.

statements.s: Gaps in a crop canopy are harmless, because sunlight is unlimited.
statements.why: Gaps in the canopy are literally unharvested photons — yield tracks how much light the canopy intercepts across the season.

activities.anchor: the water level is set by the shortest stave
activities.caption: find the limiting stave on the scale
activities.name: agLiebigPlace

config.prompt: A field is short on phosphorus but has plenty of nitrogen, water and light. Place the marker on the value that Liebig's law says actually sets this crop's growth.
config.why: Growth is limited by the scarcest resource, not the total: phosphorus, the barely-filled stave, sets the water level. Piling on nitrogen when phosphorus is short wastes both.

activities.anchor: a kilo of nitrogen buys 50 kg of grain
activities.caption: guess the nitrogen price before you read it
activities.name: agNpriceEstimate

config.prompt: The worked example sets wheat at £180 per tonne. Where the curve is steep, a kilo of nitrogen buys 50 kg of grain — worth £9. Roughly what does that kilo of nitrogen cost?
config.why: About £0.80. That is why you apply at the steep part: £9 of grain for £0.80 of nitrogen. Where the curve flattens to 4 kg of grain per kilo of nitrogen — worth £0.72 — the last kilo costs more than it returns.
config.context: £9 of grain against £0.80 of nutrient — an eleven-fold return at the steep part of the curve.

activities.anchor: Economically optimal fertiliser is
activities.caption: decide like the farm's accountant
activities.name: agMarginalBranch

config.root: Wheat sells for £180/t and a kilo of nitrogen costs about £0.80. You are standing at the point where the response curve has flattened to 4 kg of grain per kilo of nitrogen. Yield is still rising. What do you do?

start.text: The next kilo would add 4 kg of grain — £0.72 of value — for £0.80 of cost.

choices.label: Apply it — total yield still rises, and more tonnes is more money
choices.feedback: Yield does rise. Revenue does not: £0.72 in, £0.80 out.

choices.label: Stop — the last kilo already costs more than it returns
choices.feedback: Marginal analysis: keep adding only while the extra yield's value exceeds the fertiliser's cost.

maxYield.text: You bought 4 kg of grain for £0.80 that the market values at £0.72. Repeat across the field and the flat part of the curve becomes a standing loss — and the surplus nitrogen leaves for the river.

stop.text: You sit at the economic optimum: the profit-maximising rate, strictly below the yield-maximising one. The flat part of the curve stays unbought by construction.

config.why: Economically optimal fertiliser is always below the agronomic maximum. A farmer chasing maximum yield is paying for output the market price cannot repay — and exporting the excess nitrogen to the river into the bargain.

activities.anchor: roughly a century per centimetre of topsoil
activities.caption: guess the rate before the reveal
activities.name: agTopsoilEstimate

config.prompt: Under natural conditions, how many years does it take to build one centimetre of topsoil?
config.why: Roughly a century per centimetre. Erosion on exposed farmland runs 10–100× faster — which is why losing topsoil is geological vandalism on a human timescale.
config.context: A centimetre a century: a hand's depth of topsoil is a millennium's work.

activities.anchor: the dark, organic-rich
activities.caption: stack the profile back into place
activities.name: agHorizonOrder

config.prompt: Soil differentiates into horizons. Put them in order from the surface downward:
items: A horizon — dark, organic-rich topsoil, the farming layer
E horizon — the leached layer, where present
B horizon — clay and minerals accumulating in the subsoil
config.why: Topsoil first, then the leached layer, then the accumulating subsoil, then parent rock. The order tells you where the biology and the farming live.

activities.anchor: Adding a little sand to a lot of clay
activities.caption: true or false — the clay-and-sand myth
activities.name: agTextureJudge

statements.s: Texture is essentially fixed — you farm the hand you are dealt.
statements.why: The sand/silt/clay proportions are set by the parent material; structure, by contrast, is where management lives.

statements.s: Adding a little sand to clay soil improves its drainage.
statements.why: It makes a dense, brick-like mix, worse than either. Fix drainage with structure — organic matter, roots, no compaction — or engineered drains.

statements.s: Ideal soil is about 45% mineral matter and 5% organic matter.
statements.why: The remaining half splits between water and air, whose proportions swing with every rain and every drying day.

statements.s: A smeared, shiny face on the spade cut is a good sign of tilth.
statements.why: It is a compaction signature. Good structure shows crumb stability, deep roots and worms in the spadeful.

activities.anchor: wheat germinates near 4
activities.caption: put maize sowing on the thermometer
activities.name: agGerminationPlace

config.prompt: Soil temperature drives germination. Place the marker where maize starts to germinate, with warmth still rising.
config.why: Wheat germinates near 4 °C, but maize wants 10 °C and rising. That is why gardeners plant by soil thermometer, not by calendar — sow when the soil, not the sky, is ready.

activities.anchor: flood/furrow (traditional, 40–60% efficient)
activities.caption: file each irrigation method by its efficiency band
activities.name: agIrrigationBuckets

config.prompt: The lesson ranks irrigation on an efficiency ladder. File each method:

items.label: drip lines to the root zone, drop by drop

config.why: Flood is traditional and lossy, sprinklers sit in the middle, and drip — Israel's breakthrough that made desert horticulture viable — delivers to the root zone at up to 95%.

activities.anchor: iron and phosphorus lock up in acid
activities.caption: diagnose before you treat
activities.name: agPhGateBranch

config.root: A crop looks pale and hungry. A pH test comes back 5.1 — below the 6.0–7.0 window — with exchangeable aluminium rising. The nutrient bag is already in the shed. What comes first?

start.text: At pH 5.1 the nutrients may be present but locked away — and below 5.5 exchangeable aluminium turns soluble and poisons roots directly.

choices.label: Apply the fertiliser now — the crop is clearly short of something
choices.feedback: Blind fertilising of an acid field is the lesson's most common small-farm waste.

choices.label: Lime the soil toward the 6.0–7.0 window, then re-test
choices.feedback: Liming acid soil precedes every fertiliser recommendation.

blind.text: You paid for nutrients the pH gate will not let the roots reach, and the aluminium is still poisoning the root tips.

lime.text: The pH gate opens: iron and phosphorus unlock, aluminium stops being soluble, and only what the soil test still flags gets bought.

config.why: Test before treating: pH, N-P-K and organic matter tests cost little. If a crop looks hungry, the real constraint is often the pH gate or the structure, not the supply.

activities.anchor: mycorrhizal threads extend root reach ten-fold
activities.caption: pair each member of the workforce with its trade
activities.name: agBiomeMatch

config.prompt: The soil biome is the workforce. Match each worker to the job:

pairs.right: build the architecture — extend root reach and pipe phosphorus to the plant
engineer the soil — drag litter down and aerate with burrows
graze the food web that releases locked nutrients

config.why: Darwin's last book was about earthworms, and he measured their casting rates with patience worthy of the subject. Mycorrhizae are damaged by deep tillage and long bare fallows.

activities.anchor: nutrients exported in eroded soil are
activities.caption: bet before the economics lands
activities.name: agErosionPredict

config.q: A field loses its topsoil to sheet erosion. What is the argument that finally moves a farm budget?
choices: Erosion is only an aesthetic problem — the lower field receives the sediment
Nutrients exported in eroded soil are fertiliser bought twice — applied, then exported
Erosion costs nothing until the subsoil is exposed completely
The sediment improves the nearest river's fertility, so the loss is recovered
config.why: Fertiliser bought twice: applied, then exported. Off-farm the sediment delivers that fertiliser to the nearest river, where it becomes the water lesson's eutrophication problem — soil conservation and water quality are the same budget.

activities.anchor: nitrogen shortage yellows the
activities.caption: read the leaf — which nutrient is missing?
activities.name: agDeficiencyBuckets

config.prompt: Deficiency reads in the leaf, and the pattern tells you which nutrient. File each symptom:

items.label: oldest leaves yellow first — the plant cannibalises old tissue
youngest leaves yellow between green veins

config.why: Nitrogen is mobile, so the plant robs old leaves for new growth — hence yellowing from the bottom up. Iron is immobile, so the youngest leaves starve first. The patterns differ because the transport biology differs.

activities.anchor: It would be - if plants could drink air
activities.caption: fill the blank — why the sea of nitrogen is useless
activities.name: agNitrogenCloze

config.text: The atmosphere is %%0%%% N₂, yet a nitrogen shortage is entirely possible. The triple bond is so stable that almost no organism can break it: until nitrogen is %%1%% into ammonium or nitrate, the sea of it overhead is as useless to a crop as air is to a fuel tank.
config.hint: The number is the same one in the paragraph's first sentence; the verb is the one from the section's title, Haber–Bosch's job.

activities.anchor: crops typically take up 30–50% of applied nitrogen
activities.caption: guess how much of the bag the crop keeps
activities.name: agUptakeEstimate

config.prompt: In the season it is applied, roughly what percentage of applied nitrogen does a crop actually take up?
config.why: 30–50%, so around 40% is the working figure. The rest leaves by four exits — leaching, volatilisation, denitrification and runoff — and managing nitrogen means managing those four exits.
config.context: Roughly six kilos in every ten leave the field by one of four exits.

activities.anchor: the <strong>economic optimum
activities.caption: which curve peaks before the ceiling?
activities.name: agNetReturnTrace

config.prompt: Yield (green in the lesson's graph) rises toward a ceiling. Which shape does net return — yield value minus nitrogen cost — follow?

curves.label: rises and flattens toward its ceiling, like yield
peaks partway and then falls away
rises in a straight line forever

config.why: Net return peaks visibly below the biological maximum and falls steeply beyond, because every extra kilogram now buys nothing and costs money. Everything between that peak and the ceiling is the flat region — nitrogen that becomes pollution, not grain.

activities.anchor: The 4R stewardship framework
activities.caption: pair each R with the practice that delivers it
activities.name: ag4RMatch

config.prompt: The 4Rs are the operating plan for staying near the response curve's peak. Match each R to its practice:

pairs.right: slow-release or inhibitor-treated forms that match crop demand
tuned to soil tests and realistic yield targets
split-dressing at tillering and stem extension, not one autumn dump
banded below the surface near roots, where uptake beats volatilisation

config.why: Right source, right rate, right time, right place. Each R attacks one of the four exits — the same programme seen from the loss side.

activities.anchor: a workable recipe holds roughly 25–30 parts carbon
activities.caption: find the faulty line in this compost recipe
activities.name: agCompostSpot

config.prompt: A student writes up the composting recipe. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: Composting is managed aerobic decomposition, and the recipe is chemistry you can smell.
A workable pile holds roughly 25–30 parts carbon to 1 part nitrogen.
Too much carbon — straw, woodchip — and the pile heats up fast and kills weed seeds.
Too much nitrogen — fresh grass, slurry — and the pile turns putrid and loses ammonia.
A well-built pile reaches 55–65 °C within days, then cures for weeks into stable humus.
config.correction: Too much carbon (straw, woodchip) and the pile stalls, nitrogen-starved — the opposite of heating up.
config.why: Carbon-rich material starves the microbes of nitrogen and the pile stalls. It is the nitrogen-rich heaps that run hot and putrid and lose ammonia.

activities.anchor: nitrogen must be fixed
activities.caption: rebuild the chain from air to bread
activities.name: agHaberOrder

config.prompt: From the atmosphere to a human meal — put the nitrogen chain in order:
items: The atmosphere holds N₂, locked by a triple bond that almost no organism can break
Nitrogen is fixed into reactive ammonium or nitrate — by lightning, by bacteria, or industrially
Haber–Bosch combines N₂ with H₂ over an iron catalyst to make ammonia fertiliser
The crop takes up 30–50% of the applied nitrogen and builds protein
The remainder leaves by leaching, volatilisation, denitrification and runoff
config.why: Synthetic nitrogen underpins roughly half the protein in human diets (Smil's estimate). The shadow side arrives last: the four exits, which are what nitrogen management actually manages.

activities.anchor: the yellowing starts on the lower leaves
activities.caption: work the diagnosis on the yellow maize
activities.name: agMaizeBranch

config.root: A maize crop goes yellow in early June. The yellowing starts on the lower leaves and runs up the midrib — the mobile-nutrient pattern, so nitrogen is the suspect. Where does the checklist start?

start.text: Pattern says nitrogen. But nitrogen can be absent, or present and lost. What is the first question?

choices.label: Is it uniform, or in patches?
choices.feedback: Patches tell you where the nitrogen went, not just that it went.

choices.label: Buy more nitrogen and spread it evenly
choices.feedback: The worked diagnosis says otherwise: premises first.

patches.text: It is in low patches. Low spots stay wet — waterlogged soil denitrifies, converting nitrate to N₂O and N₂.

choices.label: Treat the drainage and the waterlogging, not just the nitrogen
choices.feedback: The patch tells you the exit: denitrification, not under-application.

choices.label: Blanket the field with extra nitrogen anyway
choices.feedback: The wet zones will lose most of it the same way.

drain.text: You are now reading the four exits instead of guessing at supply. A tissue test confirms 2.4% N in leaf — below sufficiency — and 40 kg/ha of injected UAN at V6 side-dresses the deficit.

blind.text: The yield map still shows the low patches: the nitrogen left by the same exit it left last time.

config.why: Diagnosis comes before treatment. Patches in low spots point to waterlogging and denitrification; unincorporated slurry points to volatilisation; and a chlorophyll meter against a reference strip quantifies whatever deficit remains.
